candidate.answerReason: Each tile changes the perimeter by an even number no greater than 2. Thus the new perimeter is even and at most 18. Extending the lower row leftward and the upper row rightward attains 18.

methods.label: Track the change in boundary edges
methods.explanation:
The useful observation is that a shared side lies inside the figure and contributes nothing to its perimeter.

Add the tiles one at a time. Suppose an added tile shares \(k\) sides with the figure already present. Its attachment removes those \(k\) sides from the old boundary and contributes its other \(4-k\) sides. The perimeter therefore changes by
\[
(4-k)-k=4-2k.
\]
Each new tile must share a side with an original tile, so \(k\geq1\), even when adding the second tile. Consequently, each addition increases the perimeter by at most \(2\), and its change is always even. Starting from \(14\), the final perimeter must be even and cannot exceed
\[
14+2+2=18.
\]
This rules out the odd choices \(15,17,19\), as well as \(20\).

We must also show that \(18\) is possible. In the displayed figure, place one tile immediately to the left of the lower row and the other immediately to the right of the upper row. Each shares exactly one side with the original figure, and they do not share a side with each other. Each therefore adds \(2\) to the perimeter.

The resulting perimeter is \(\boxed{18}\) units, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument counts unit boundary edges, uses even numbers, and exhibits a concrete placement. No advanced counting machinery is needed.
